description: We are a team of 4 unofficially representing the Heritage High School team. We are all Interested in Rocketry, Astronomy, and Computer Science, as well as the wonders of the far unknown of deep space.
summary: Hullo is a website for ages 10 to 14 about the hardware NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Students fire a laser at an Apollo mirror, replay Ingenuity's 72 flights and message Voyager 1, with real NASA data setting every answer. Kids mostly hear about missions still running, and Hullo gives them a reason to care about the rest.
details:
What Hullo does

Hullo is a ten page website for ages 10 to 14 about the hardware NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. The site opens with a photo story of five machines, from Surveyor 3 in 1967 to Ingenuity in 2021. Every page after that gives students something to do with real NASA numbers.

Live

The Live page shows how far away Voyager 1 is this second. On 15 November 2026 Voyager 1 was 25,896,821,943 km from Earth. Light takes 23 hours 59 minutes to cover that distance, which put Voyager 1 about two days short of one full light-day.

The same page reads NASA's DSN Now feed every 8 seconds and shows which Deep Space Network dish is talking to which spacecraft.

Moon

Students fire a laser at one of the five mirrors that Apollo 11, Apollo 14, Apollo 15, Lunokhod 1 and Lunokhod 2 left on the Moon. The echo comes back after the real light time. On 15 November 2026 the Moon was 397,690 km away and the echo took 2.7 seconds.

Mars

NASA built Ingenuity for 5 flights and the helicopter flew 72. Students step through every flight with its date, distance, height and time in the air. Flight 9 covered 625 m in 166.4 seconds.

A chart compares the distance and height of all 72 flights.

Orbit

The Orbit page marks the Apollo and Mars landing sites on maps of the Moon and Mars and counts the days since each landing. Apollo 11 landed 20,938 days before 15 November 2026. Students can also play a marsquake recorded by InSight, which felt 1,319 marsquakes.

Deep space

Students send a pretend message to Voyager 1, Voyager 2, New Horizons, Pioneer 10 or Pioneer 11. The message travels at the speed of light, so a hullo to Voyager 1 arrives about a day later.

The silent ones

This page lists 22 pieces of NASA hardware with their launch and last contact dates. Six are still active and 16 have ended.

Passport and Classroom

Each activity earns a stamp. The Passport holds 31 stamps and prints a certificate. The Classroom page has three printable worksheets with answer keys, filled in with the site's numbers at the moment of printing.

How it works

Hullo is a static site with no server and no login. Python scripts fetch positions from JPL Horizons, and the browser works out the light time every second. 69 automated tests check the maths and the sources. The Sources page lists 75 sources with their links, dates and licenses, and credits every photo.

Benefits

A teacher can run a lesson with no accounts and nothing to install. Hullo works on a phone. Names and stamps stay on the student's device.

Tools

Astro, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, visx, MapLibre GL, wavesurfer.js and Python. Netlify hosts the site.

How it is creative

Students wait the real light time. A laser comes back from the Moon in under 3 seconds and a message to Voyager 1 takes about a day, so students feel the size of the solar system.

What we considered

Accuracy came first, with a source for every number. The text is short, for ages 10 to 14. Every photo is a NASA original shown with its credit, and the site uses no NASA logos. The project shows no names or photos of the team, because we are under 18.
